topic.name: The Chain Rule With Trigonometric Functions

question.explanation:
First, we express

\[ f(x) = (\sin{x})^2. \]

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

\[ f = u^2, \qquad u=\sin x. \]

Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 2u \qquad \style{font-family:inherit;}{\text{and}} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=2u\cdot \cos{x}\\[5pt] &=2\sin{x}\cos{x}. \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = 2\sec{u}, \qquad u = 6x - 2. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 2\sec u \tan u, \qquad\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 6. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} & = \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=2\sec u \tan u \cdot 6\\[5pt] &=12\sec u \tan u\\[5pt] &=12\sec(6x-2)\tan(6x-2) \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = 3\sec{u}, \qquad u = \cos{x}. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 3\sec{u} \tan u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin{x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=3\sec{u} \tan u \cdot (-\sin x)\\[5pt] &=-3\sin x\sec{\left(\cos x\right)} \tan \left(\cos x\right). \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express \[ f(x) = -4(\cos{(x)})^{5}. \]

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function \[ f = -4u^{5}, \qquad u = \cos{(x)}. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm d u} = -20u^4, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin{(x)}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get \begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] & = -20u^4 \cdot (-\sin{(x)})\\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{20\cos^4{(x)}\sin{(x)}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =3\sin \left(\cos x \right)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right).$
question.explanation:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is given by $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function \[ f = 3\sin(u), \qquad u = \cos(x). \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 3\cos(u), \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-\sin(x). \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=3\cos(u) \cdot (-\sin(x)) \\[5pt] &=-3\sin(x)\cos\left(\cos(x)\right). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we find \[ \eqalign{ f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)&=-3\sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} \cos{\left(\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)}\right)} \\[5pt] &=-3(1)(1) \\[5pt] % &=-3\cdot 1 \\[5pt] &=-3. } \]

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right) \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\[3pt] y-0 &= -3\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\\[3pt] y&=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-3x + \dfrac{3\pi}{2}} \end{align}
